lesson.title: How Fast Is a Population Really Growing?
lesson.summary: When a population grows exponentially, its growth rate is not constant, it is proportional to the population itself, and the derivative reveals exactly that relationship.
lesson.body:
Many populations that are not yet limited by resources, a bacteria colony in a fresh dish, a cell culture, an early stage outbreak, grow according to the exponential model P(t) = P0 * e^(k t), where P0 is the initial population, k is a constant growth rate, and t is time. This is a direct instance of the derivative in context process: P is the dependent variable measured in a count of individuals, t is the independent variable measured in time, and differentiating will produce a rate measured in individuals per unit time.

Differentiating the general model gives P'(t) = P0 * k * e^(k t), which can be rewritten as P'(t) = k * P(t), since P0 * e^(k t) is just P(t) itself. This is the single most important fact about exponential growth: the growth rate is proportional to the current population, not to time. A colony twice as large grows twice as fast in absolute terms, even though the fractional growth rate k stays fixed. That proportionality is exactly why exponential growth feels slow at first and then explosive later: more individuals means more simultaneous reproduction.

Consider a bacteria colony with P(t) = 1000 * e^(0.05 t), where P is measured in bacteria and t in hours. Differentiating gives P'(t) = 1000 * 0.05 * e^(0.05 t) = 50 * e^(0.05 t) bacteria per hour. At t = 0, P'(0) = 50 bacteria per hour: the colony starts out gaining 50 bacteria every hour. At t = 20 hours, P(20) = 1000 * e^1 is approximately 2718 bacteria, and P'(20) = 50 * e^1 is approximately 135.9 bacteria per hour. Checking the proportionality: k * P(20) = 0.05 * 2718.3, which is approximately 135.9, matching P'(20) exactly, as it must.

Real populations rarely grow exponentially forever, since resources eventually limit them, but the same algebra handles decline just as well. If k is negative instead, say k = -0.02, the formula P(t) = P0 * e^(k t) models a population that is shrinking, and P'(t) = k * P(t) is now negative because k is negative while P(t) stays positive, correctly signaling a decreasing count. Reading that sign and those units is exactly the rate interpretation skill from two chapters back, now applied to a living, changing population.
